Aṅguttara-Nikāya. XI.

Just as, venerable sir, a dust-cloth wipes clean things and wipes dirty things, wipes away excrement and wipes away urine, wipes away saliva, wipes away pus, and wipes away blood, and the dust-cloth is neither troubled nor disgusted by it; just so, venerable sir, I dwell with a mind like a dust-cloth, expansive, exalted, measureless, free from enmity, free from ill-will. Whoever, venerable sir, does not have mindfulness directed toward the body established in their own body, such a person might offend a fellow practitioner and depart on their journey without having made amends.

Just as, venerable sir, an outcaste boy or an outcaste girl, with a basket in hand, wearing ragged clothes <note>original: "nantikavāsī"</note>, enters a village or a town with a lowly mind; just so, venerable sir, I dwell with a mind like an outcaste boy, expansive, exalted, measureless, free from enmity, free from ill-will. Whoever, venerable sir, does not have mindfulness directed toward the body established in their own body, such a person might offend a fellow practitioner and depart on their journey without having made amends.

Just as, venerable sir, a bull with broken horns, gentle, well-tamed, and well-trained, wandering from street to street and crossroads to crossroads, harms no one with its feet or its horns; just so, venerable sir, I dwell with a mind like a bull with broken horns, expansive, exalted, measureless, free from enmity, free from ill-will. Whoever, venerable sir, does not have mindfulness directed toward the body established in their own body, such a person might offend a fellow practitioner and depart on their journey without having made amends.
